raw_response:
I am seventy years old, and my bones know every inch of this land. Fifty years of farming in Quzhou has taught me that at my age, with just my wife and me, I must work *with* the seasons, not against them. I have six mu and a reliable well, so water is not my worry—labor is.

My mainstay is the **cabbage-maize-spinach** rotation that has fed my family and paid for my grandchildren’s schooling. I will put **three mu into spring cabbage**—transplanting *Zhonggan 56* in March, because it is a proven hybrid that resists soft rot and gives me about 8,000 jin per mu. I will rotary-till the beds, lay down a basal compound fertilizer, and irrigate five times with border irrigation from my well. After I harvest that cabbage in late May, I will immediately sow **summer maize** on the same three mu. I use *Denghai 605* and plant it no-tillage—no point in breaking my back tilling soil that is already loose, and it keeps the moisture in for the June heat. Two irrigations and two careful pesticide sprays are enough for maize if you watch it daily. Come October, when the maize is dry in the stalk, I will sow **winter spinach** on those three mu. It is a hardy crop that needs little care through the cold months and brings a good price before the Spring Festival.

The second cabbage I mentioned is **autumn cabbage** on **two mu**. I will plant it in August and harvest in November. This land has been resting since winter, and the soil is eager. I keep the inputs similar to spring cabbage but slightly less irrigation because the autumn rains in Hebei usually help.

For cash, I keep **half a mu of chili** and **half a mu of kidney bean**. Chili is labor-heavy—I must spray for aphids and diseases almost every week in the hot months—but the price at the Quzhou market is too good to give up entirely. I limit myself to half a mu so my wife and I can manage the twelve sprayings without hiring help. The kidney bean is quicker, maturing by August, and it fills the gap before the autumn cabbage needs my full attention.

I am educated enough to know that balanced fertilization pays. I use compound fertilizer as a basal dose and top-dress with urea when the plants tell me they are hungry. I do not chase maximum yield anymore; I chase *stable* yield with my own two hands.
